claim: The dorsolateral striatum (DLS) is especially implicated in habitual and skilled performance.
source: Hypotheses of striatal orchestration of behavior ascribe distinct functions to striatal subregions, with the dorsolateral striatum (DLS) especially implicated in habitual and skilled performance.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work in the field.

claim: Clear changes in corresponding neural activity patterns were not evident in DMS or DLS during early training despite improving performance across sessions.
source: Despite improving performance across sessions, clear changes in corresponding neural activity patterns were not evident in DMS or DLS during early training.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's data analysis.

claim: DMS and DLS activity patterns were distinct during early training.
source: Although DMS and DLS activity patterns were distinct during early training, their activity was similar following extended training.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's data analysis.

claim: DMS and DLS activity was similar following extended training.
source: Although DMS and DLS activity patterns were distinct during early training, their activity was similar following extended training.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's data analysis.

claim: Performance after extended training was not associated with DMS disengagement.
source: Finally, performance after extended training was not associated with DMS disengagement, as would be predicted from prior work.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's data analysis.

claim: Behavioral sequences may continue to engage both striatal regions long after initial acquisition, when skilled performance is consolidated.
source: These results suggest that behavioral sequences may continue to engage both striatal regions long after initial acquisition, when skilled performance is consolidated.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: The dorsomedial striatum (DMS) receives excitatory inputs from prefrontal cortices and is implicated in goal-directed action control.
source: The dorsomedial striatum (DMS) receives excitatory inputs from prefrontal cortices and is implicated in goal-directed action control, whereas the dorsolateral striatum (DLS) primarily receives inputs from sensorimotor and premotor cortices and is implicated in habit and skill learning (Balleine et al., 2009; Corbit and Janak, 2016; Corbit et al., 2007; Corbit and Janak, 2010; Graybiel and Grafton, 2015; Yin and Knowlton, 2006; Yin et al., 2004; Yin et al., 2005; Yin and Knowlton, 2006; Yin et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: The dorsolateral striatum (DLS) primarily receives inputs from sensorimotor and premotor cortices and is implicated in habit and skill learning.
source: The dorsomedial striatum (DMS) receives excitatory inputs from prefrontal cortices and is implicated in goal-directed action control, whereas the dorsolateral striatum (DLS) primarily receives inputs from sensorimotor and premotor cortices and is implicated in habit and skill learning (Balleine et al., 2009; Corbit and Janak, 2016; Corbit et al., 2007; Corbit and Janak, 2010; Graybiel and Grafton, 2015; Yin and Knowlton, 2006; Yin et al., 2004; Yin et al., 2005; Yin and Knowlton, 2006; Yin et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Neuronal excitations emerge over learning in the dorsal striatum at the initiation and termination of the response sequence when subjects are trained to execute a series of lever presses for reward.
source: When subjects are trained to execute a series of lever presses for reward, neuronal excitations emerge over learning in the dorsal striatum at the initiation and termination of the response sequence (Jin and Costa, 2010; Jin et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Neural excitations at the start and stop of sequences, along with sustained inhibitions and excitations, are proposed to reflect chunking of individual actions into behavioral units.
source: These neural excitations have been termed start/stop responses, and, along with sustained inhibitions and excitations, are proposed to reflect chunking of individual actions into behavioral units (Jin and Costa, 2015; Jin and Costa, 2010; Jin et al., 2014; Martiros et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Sequence-related neural responses are reported to be more numerous in the DLS.
source: These sequence-related neural responses are reported to be more numerous in the DLS (Martiros et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Contrasting patterns of neural ensemble activity emerge in the DMS and DLS as rats learn to choose the correct arm of a T-maze in response to sensory cue presentations.
source: Consistent with this, contrasting patterns of neural ensemble activity emerge in the DMS and DLS as rats learn to choose the correct arm of a T-maze in response to sensory cue presentations (Barnes et al., 2005; Thorn et al., 2010), with task-bracketing activity emerging in the DLS (Barnes et al., 2005; Jog et al., 1999; Smith and Graybiel, 2016; Thorn et al., 2010), but not in the DMS.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Task-bracketing activity emerges in the DLS but not in the DMS during T-maze learning.
source: Consistent with this, contrasting patterns of neural ensemble activity emerge in the DMS and DLS as rats learn to choose the correct arm of a T-maze in response to sensory cue presentations (Barnes et al., 2005; Thorn et al., 2010), with task-bracketing activity emerging in the DLS (Barnes et al., 2005; Jog et al., 1999; Smith and Graybiel, 2016; Thorn et al., 2010), but not in the DMS.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The presence of task-bracketing neuronal activity around actions made to obtain reward is not always detected.
source: However, the presence of task-bracketing neuronal activity around actions made to obtain reward is not always detected (Sales-Carbonell et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Responding for sucrose reward rapidly becomes habitual when lever insertion and retraction cues are provided in the discrete-trials fixed-ratio 5 (DT5) task.
source: We previously showed that responding for sucrose reward rapidly becomes habitual when the lever insertion and retraction cues are provided in this discrete-trials fixed-ratio 5 (DT5) task; in contrast, responding remains sensitive to reward devaluation, a test of goal-directed control, in absence of these cues under a free-running fixed-ratio five schedule (Vandaele et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the authors' prior work.

claim: Responding remains sensitive to reward devaluation in absence of lever insertion and retraction cues under a free-running fixed-ratio five schedule.
source: We previously showed that responding for sucrose reward rapidly becomes habitual when the lever insertion and retraction cues are provided in this discrete-trials fixed-ratio 5 (DT5) task; in contrast, responding remains sensitive to reward devaluation, a test of goal-directed control, in absence of these cues under a free-running fixed-ratio five schedule (Vandaele et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the authors' prior work.

claim: Lever pressing remained near the maximum possible (150 responses/session) throughout training.
source: Throughout training, lever pressing remained near the maximum possible (150 responses/session) (Figure 1C), yet performance become more automated across sessions in the early training group, indicative of sequence learning (Figure 1D–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Performance became more automated across sessions in the early training group, indicative of sequence learning.
source: Throughout training, lever pressing remained near the maximum possible (150 responses/session) (Figure 1C), yet performance become more automated across sessions in the early training group, indicative of sequence learning (Figure 1D–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 1D-G.

claim: The number of within-sequence reward port entries was rapidly suppressed across sessions (Friedman ANOVA χ2 = 44.82, p<0.0001).
source: Specifically, the number of within-sequence reward port entries was rapidly suppressed across sessions (Friedman ANOVA χ2 = 44.82, p<0.0001; Figure 1D), including in the first DT5 session, as subjects learned the response requirement had increased from one to five.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Learning was accompanied by a progressive increase in response rate (F(9,72)=16.59, p<0.0001).
source: Learning was also accompanied by a progressive increase in response rate (Figure 1E; F(9,72)=16.59, p<0.0001) and a concomitant decrease in trial-by-trial variability in within-sequence response rate (Figure 1F; F(9,72)=3.12, p<0.01).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Learning was accompanied by a concomitant decrease in trial-by-trial variability in within-sequence response rate (F(9,72)=3.12, p<0.01).
source: Learning was also accompanied by a progressive increase in response rate (Figure 1E; F(9,72)=16.59, p<0.0001) and a concomitant decrease in trial-by-trial variability in within-sequence response rate (Figure 1F; F(9,72)=3.12, p<0.01).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The latency to first lever press decreased across early training sessions (F(12,96)=10.87, p<0.0001).
source: The latency to first lever press also decreased across early training sessions (Figure 1G; F(12,96)=10.87, p<0.0001).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Following extended training, within-sequence port entries did not differ from zero.
source: Following extended training in the second group of rats, within-sequence port entries did not differ from zero and response rate, trial-by-trial variability in response rate and the latency to first lever press reached a plateau (Figure 1C–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 1C-G.

claim: Response rate, trial-by-trial variability in response rate and the latency to first lever press reached a plateau following extended training.
source: Following extended training in the second group of rats, within-sequence port entries did not differ from zero and response rate, trial-by-trial variability in response rate and the latency to first lever press reached a plateau (Figure 1C–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 1C-G.

claim: Mean responding decreased following devaluation, but this decrease was not significant after either early or extended training when analyzing the number of lever presses (early training: F(1,8)=4.87, p=0.06; extended training: F(1,7)=3.75, p=0.09).
source: While mean responding decreased following devaluation, this decrease was not significant after either early or extended training when analyzing the number of lever presses (Figure 1H; early training: F(1,8)=4.87, p=0.06; extended training: F(1,7)=3.75, p=0.09) or the number of trial initiated (Figure 1I; early training: F(1,8)=4.25, p=0.07; extended training: F(1,7)=3.5, p>0.1), suggesting that behavior was under habitual control, although there was variability within the groups.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: The decrease in responding following devaluation was not significant when analyzing the number of trials initiated (early training: F(1,8)=4.25, p=0.07; extended training: F(1,7)=3.5, p>0.1).
source: While mean responding decreased following devaluation, this decrease was not significant after either early or extended training when analyzing the number of lever presses (Figure 1H; early training: F(1,8)=4.87, p=0.06; extended training: F(1,7)=3.75, p=0.09) or the number of trial initiated (Figure 1I; early training: F(1,8)=4.25, p=0.07; extended training: F(1,7)=3.5, p>0.1), suggesting that behavior was under habitual control, although there was variability within the groups.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: The lack of significant devaluation effect suggests that behavior was under habitual control, although there was variability within the groups.
source: While mean responding decreased following devaluation, this decrease was not significant after either early or extended training when analyzing the number of lever presses (Figure 1H; early training: F(1,8)=4.87, p=0.06; extended training: F(1,7)=3.75, p=0.09) or the number of trial initiated (Figure 1I; early training: F(1,8)=4.25, p=0.07; extended training: F(1,7)=3.5, p>0.1), suggesting that behavior was under habitual control, although there was variability within the groups.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the statistical results.

claim: During acquisition of the task in the early training group, an average of 37 (±1.3) and 81 (±1.8) units per session were recorded in the DLS and DMS, respectively.
source: During acquisition of the task in the early training group, we recorded an average of 37 (±1.3) and 81 (±1.8) units per session in the DLS and DMS, respectively, across the entire group of rats.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the study.

claim: The number of recorded units remained stable across sessions.
source: The number of recorded units remained stable across sessions (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: In the extended training group, a total of 387 and 462 neurons were recorded in DLS and DMS, respectively.
source: In the extended training group, by advancing the electrodes every other day, a total of 387 and 462 neurons were recorded in DLS and DMS, respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Putative MSNs represented 95% and 88% of the recorded units in the early and extended training groups, respectively.
source: Putative MSNs represented 95% and 88% of the recorded units in the early and extended training groups, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the study.

claim: Fast-spiking interneurons (FSI) represented on average 1.1% of units in the early training group and 4.1% of units in the extended training group.
source: Fast-spiking interneurons (FSI) were extracted based on their firing rate and half-width valley (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D–F), and represented on average 1.1% of units in the early training group (0–3 neurons per session) and 4.1% of units in the extended training group (N = 31).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the study.

claim: On average, 78.2% (±1.4) of putative MSNs from the early training dataset showed a significant change in firing rate to one or more events, and were termed task-responsive neurons (TRN).
source: On average, 78.2% (±1.4) of putative MSNs from the early training dataset showed a significant change in firing rate to one or more events, and were termed task-responsive neurons (TRN) (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: A majority of DLS neurons increased their spike activity during the behavioral sequence (excitation, range N = 15–24 per session; inhibition, range N = 4–9 per session).
source: Among them, a majority of DLS neurons increased their spike activity during the behavioral sequence (excitation, range N = 15–24 per session; inhibition, range N = 4–9 per session) whereas DMS neurons predominantly decreased their spike activity (excitation, range N = 13–21 per session; inhibition, range N = 34–61 per session).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the study.

claim: DMS neurons predominantly decreased their spike activity during the behavioral sequence (excitation, range N = 13–21 per session; inhibition, range N = 34–61 per session).
source: Among them, a majority of DLS neurons increased their spike activity during the behavioral sequence (excitation, range N = 15–24 per session; inhibition, range N = 4–9 per session) whereas DMS neurons predominantly decreased their spike activity (excitation, range N = 13–21 per session; inhibition, range N = 34–61 per session).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the study.

claim: The relative proportions of excitations and inhibitions significantly differed between DLS and DMS for the ten sessions analyzed during early training (DLS vs DMS, χ2-values > 7.2, p-values<0.01).
source: The relative proportions of excitations and inhibitions significantly differed between DLS and DMS for the ten sessions analyzed during early training (Figure 2A; DLS vs DMS, χ2-values > 7.2, p-values<0.01).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: In the extended training dataset, 76.5% of the analyzed neurons were task-responsive.
source: In the extended training dataset, 76.5% of the analyzed neurons were task-responsive.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the study.

claim: The number of neurons excited and inhibited during the behavioral sequence was similar in DLS versus DMS after extended training (DLS excitation, N = 143; DLS inhibition, N = 109; DMS excitation, N = 158; DMS inhibition, N = 162; DMS vs DLS: χ2 = 3.07, p>0.05).
source: In clear contrast with the early training group, the number of neurons excited and inhibited during the behavioral sequence was similar in DLS versus DMS (Figure 2A; DLS excitation, N = 143; DLS inhibition, N = 109; DMS excitation, N = 158; DMS inhibition, N = 162; DMS vs DLS: χ2 = 3.07, p>0.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: During early training, the DLS population showed a sustained increase in activity throughout the behavioral sequence whereas the mean activity for the DMS population was increased at the sequence boundaries and decreased during lever presses.
source: During early training, we observed strong differences between the activity of TRN in DLS and DMS along the behavioral sequence. On average, the DLS population showed a sustained increase in activity throughout the behavioral sequence whereas the mean activity for the DMS population was increased at the sequence boundaries and decreased during lever presses (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 2A-B.

claim: Repeated measures ANOVA revealed differences between regions and across events during early training (main effect of region, F(1,839)=135.1, p<0.0001; region * event interaction, F(11,9229) = 30.85, p<0.0001).
source: Repeated measures ANOVA revealed differences between regions and across events (Figure 2B and D; main effect of region, F(1,839)=135.1, p<0.0001; region * event interaction, F(11,9229) = 30.85, p<0.0001).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figures 2B and D.

claim: When mean neural activity was examined after extended training, the differences in DMS and DLS population activity were not significant, with no effect of region, nor a region by event interaction (region F(1,570)=2.53, p>0.1, region*event F(11,6270) = 1.48, p>0.1).
source: When mean neural activity was examined after extended training, the differences in DMS and DLS population activity were not significant, with no effect of region, nor a region by event interaction (Figure 2C and E; region F(1,570)=2.53, p>0.1, region*event F(11,6270) = 1.48, p>0.1).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figures 2C and E.

claim: There was no significant change in mean normalized activity in DMS and DLS across early training sessions despite significant performance improvements during the task (main effect of session, F(9,839)=0.49, p>0.1; session*event interaction, F(99,9229) = 0.72, p>0.1).
source: Surprisingly, there was no significant change in mean normalized activity in DMS and DLS across early training sessions despite significant performance improvements during the task (Figure 1D–G; Figure 2B and D, top versus bottom panels; main effect of session, F(9,839)=0.49, p>0.1; session*event interaction, F(99,9229) = 0.72, p>0.1).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figures 1D-G and 2B, D.

claim: An increase in DLS neural activity in the 500 ms before the first lever press was observed across DT1 sessions (Wilcoxon test, 1st vs 3rd DT1: Z = −2.29, p<0.05; 1st DT1 vs 1st DT5: Z = −2.16, p<0.05).
source: Here we observed an increase in DLS neural activity in the 500 ms before the first lever press across DT1 sessions (Figure 2—figure supplement 2; Wilcoxon test, 1st vs 3rd DT1: Z = −2.29, p<0.05; 1st DT1 vs 1st DT5: Z = −2.16, p<0.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Many neurons showed transient changes in activity (<0.25 s; termed 'Phasic') while many others expressed excitations or inhibitions that were sustained in time (>0.5 s; 'Non-phasic').
source: First, we observed that many neurons showed transient changes in activity (<0.25 s; termed 'Phasic') while many others expressed excitations or inhibitions that were sustained in time (>0.5 s; 'Non-phasic').
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the study.

claim: Hierarchical clustering on the combined DMS and DLS dataset resulted in two significant classes of neurons: Phasic neurons (N = 635) and Non-phasic neurons (N = 113).
source: This method resulted in two significant classes of neurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 1; permutation test, p<0.0001). The majority of neurons were characterized by transient peaks of activity at some time in the behavioral sequence, and were classified as Phasic neurons (N = 635; Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1). Neurons from the other class mostly expressed sustained activity throughout the lever press sequence and were classified as Non-phasic neurons (N = 113; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The proportion of Phasic versus Non-phasic neurons did not significantly differ between brain regions (χ2 = 0.39, p>0.1).
source: The proportion of Phasic versus Non-phasic neurons did not significantly differ between brain regions (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C; χ2 = 0.39, p>0.1).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Hierarchical clustering applied to the combined set of DMS and DLS Phasic neurons resulted in the separation of 3 significant classes of neurons: Start neurons (DLS N = 46, DMS N = 64), Stop neurons (DLS N = 72, DMS N = 91), and Middle neurons (DLS N = 172, DMS N = 190).
source: Hierarchical clustering applied to the combined set of DMS and DLS Phasic neurons resulted in the separation of 3 significant classes of neurons (Figure 3B): neurons expressing transient excitations after the lever insertion ('Start' neurons, DLS N = 46, DMS N = 64; Figure 3C), before the port entry ('Stop' neurons, DLS N = 72, DMS N = 91; Figure 3D) or modulations at one or more points during the lever presses ('Middle' neurons, DLS N = 172, DMS N = 190; Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 3B-E.

claim: The proportions of neurons in each Phasic class and their average z-scores did not significantly differ between DLS and DMS (χ2 = 1.3, p > 0.1; region: F-values < 3.5, p-values > 0.05; region*events: F-values < 2.1, p-values > 0.05).
source: The proportions of neurons in each Phasic class and their average z-scores did not significantly differ between DLS and DMS (χ2 = 1.3, p > 0.1; region: F-values < 3.5, p-values > 0.05; region*events: F-values < 2.1, p-values > 0.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of data from the study.

claim: Only 15% of Phasic Start neurons (16/110 units) increase their spiking activity prior to the first lever press relative to baseline.
source: Statistical analysis of spiking activity revealed that only 15% of Phasic Start neurons (16/110 units) increase their spiking activity prior to the first lever press relative to baseline (i.e., at the presumed time of sequence initiation) (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The Phasic Start neurons responding to the lever insertion cue are not explicitly signaling motor sequence initiation.
source: These results suggest that, in the main, the Phasic Start neurons responding to the lever insertion cue are not explicitly signaling motor sequence initiation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Phasic Stop neurons increased activity after the last lever press with an even greater peak before the port entry.
source: Phasic Stop neurons increased activity after the last lever press with an even greater peak before the port entry (Figure 4C), that is, before consumption of the reward.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The port entry peak in Phasic Stop neurons was not observed during port entries occurring during inter-trial intervals.
source: This port entry peak was not observed during port entries occurring during inter-trial intervals (Figure 4D), suggesting that this activity may encode termination of the sequence and/or reward expectation during the port approach.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The activity of Phasic Stop neurons may encode termination of the sequence and/or reward expectation during the port approach.
source: This port entry peak was not observed during port entries occurring during inter-trial intervals (Figure 4D), suggesting that this activity may encode termination of the sequence and/or reward expectation during the port approach.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Hierarchical clustering on Non-phasic neurons resulted in the separation of 2 significant classes of neurons: INH neurons (DLS N = 17/48, 35%; DMS N = 36/65, 55%) and EXC neurons (DLS N = 31/48, 64%; DMS N = 29/65, 45%).
source: This analysis resulted in the separation of 2 significant classes of neurons (Figure 5B–D): neurons expressing sustained inhibition ('INH' neurons, DLS N = 17/48, 35%; DMS N = 36/65, 55%; Figure 5C) or sustained excitation during the five lever presses ('EXC' neurons, DLS N = 31/48, 64%; DMS N = 29/65, 45%; Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 5B-D.

claim: The proportion of neurons across the Non-phasic classes significantly differed between DLS and DMS (χ2 = 4.4, p<0.05) with a higher proportion of EXC neurons in DLS compared to DMS.
source: The proportion of neurons across the Non-phasic classes did significantly differ between DLS and DMS (χ2 = 4.4, p<0.05) with a higher proportion of EXC neurons in DLS compared to DMS (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: In each Non-phasic class, the average normalized activity of DMS and DLS neurons did not differ across events in the behavioral sequence (region*event, INH F(11,561) = 0.41, p>0.1, EXC F(11,638) = 1.56, p>0.1).
source: In each class, the average normalized activity of DMS and DLS neurons did not differ across events in the behavioral sequence (region*event, INH F(11,561) = 0.41, p>0.1, EXC F(11,638) = 1.56, p>0.1).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of data from the study.

claim: The proportion of Phasic and Non-phasic neurons in each session did not differ in DLS and DMS (χ2 <2.9, p-values>0.05).
source: The proportion of Phasic and Non-phasic neurons in each session did not differ in DLS and DMS (χ2 <2.9, p-values>0.05; Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The proportion of neurons in Phasic classes was similar between DLS and DMS for most sessions (χ2 <4.4, p-values>0.1), except the 4th session.
source: The proportion of neurons in Phasic classes was similar between DLS and DMS for most sessions (χ2 <4.4, p-values>0.1), except the 4th session, where there was a greater fraction of Stop neurons and fewer Middle neurons in DLS (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Neurons in Non-phasic classes were differentially distributed in DLS versus DMS in every session (χ2-values > 5.5, p-values<0.05).
source: On the other hand, neurons in Non-phasic classes were differentially distributed in DLS versus DMS in every session (χ2-values > 5.5, p-values<0.05; Figure 6E).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The majority (on average, 83%) of DLS Non-phasic neurons were classified as EXC whereas only an average of 21% of DMS non-phasic neurons were.
source: More specifically, the majority (on average, 83%) of DLS Non-phasic neurons were classified as EXC whereas only an average of 21% of DMS non-phasic neurons were.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the study.

claim: DMS Non-phasic neurons were much more represented in the INH class.
source: DMS Non-phasic neurons were much more represented in the INH class (Figure 6E–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 6E-G.

claim: There was no significant change in class proportions across sessions (DLS, χ2 = 39, p>0.1; DMS, χ2 = 41, p>0.1).
source: We found no significant change in class proportions across sessions (DLS, χ2 = 39, p>0.1; DMS, χ2 = 41, p>0.1).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of data from the study.

claim: There was no evidence for changes in normalized activity across early training sessions (session F-values <1.4, p-values>0.1; session*event F-values <1.2, p-values>0.1).
source: Analayzing the normalized activity of all units in a given class, we also obtained no evidence for changes across early training sessions (session F-values <1.4, p-values>0.1; session*event F-values <1.2, p-values>0.1; Figure 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 6.

claim: ANOVAs detected regional differences in the magnitude of the mean normalized activity within the Start, Stop and Middle populations of neurons when comparing DMS and DLS (Start neurons: region F(1,191)=91.3, p<0.0001; region*event: F(11,2101) = 20.08, p<0.0001; Stop neurons: region F(1,112)=13.65, p<0.001; region*event F(11,1232) = 5.62, p<0.01; Middle neurons: region F(1,433)=63.89, p<0.0001; region*event F(11,4763) = 9.71, p<0.0001).
source: These ANOVAs however did detect regional differences in the magnitude of the mean normalized activity within the Start, Stop and Middle populations of neurons when comparing DMS and DLS (Start neurons: region F(1,191)=91.3, p<0.0001; region*event: F(11,2101) = 20.08, p<0.0001; Stop neurons: region F(1,112)=13.65, p<0.001; region*event F(11,1232) = 5.62, p<0.01; Middle neurons: region F(1,433)=63.89, p<0.0001; region*event F(11,4763) = 9.71, p<0.0001; Figure 6B–D), reflecting higher average firing in DLS during lever presses, and higher activity after lever insertion and retraction in the DMS.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figures 6B-D.

claim: LDA models accurately revealed brain region identity during early training with mean accuracy for assignment to DMS or DLS significantly above chance for all early training sessions (p-values<0.0001, permutation test).
source: LDA models accurately revealed brain region identity during early training. More specifically, mean accuracy for assignment to DMS or DLS was significantly above chance for all early training sessions (p-values<0.0001, permutation test; Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: For extended training, decoding accuracy did not differ from chance, even for the largest ensemble size (p-values>0.05, permutation test).
source: In contrast, for extended training, decoding accuracy did not differ from chance, even for the largest ensemble size (p-values>0.05, permutation test; Figure 7A).

claim: DMS and DLS neurons cannot be differentiated based on their sequence-related activity after extended training.
source: These results demonstrate that DMS and DLS neurons cannot be differentiated based on their sequence-related activity after extended training.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the decoding analysis results.

claim: Using PCA and LDA models trained on the first three principal components, decoding accuracy was significantly above chance in all early training sessions (all p-values<0.0001, permutation test) but not for extended training, even for larger sets of units (all p-values>0.05, permutation test).

claim: Repeated measures ANOVA examining average normalized activity of DMS and DLS neurons along the behavioral sequence across early training sessions revealed significant region by group and region by group by event interactions (region*group: F(1,819)=22.36, p<0.0001; region*group*event: F(11,9009) = 4.3, p<0.01), but no main effect of group (F(1,819)=0.69,p>0.4) nor event by group interaction (F(11,9009) = 1.24,p>0.2).
source: Examining the average normalized activity of DMS and DLS neurons along the behavioral sequence across early training sessions (Figure 8A), we observed significant region by group and region by group by event interactions during early training (region*group: F(1,819)=22.36, p<0.0001; region*group*event: F(11,9009) = 4.3, p<0.01), but no main effect of group (F(1,819)=0.69,p>0.4) nor event by group interaction (F(11,9009) = 1.24,p>0.2).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: When looking at the normalized activity in DMS and DLS in rats more or less sensitive to outcome devaluation during extended training, no significant differences were found (main effect of group: F(1,568)=2.84, p>0.05; group*region interaction: F(1,568)=1.32, p>0.1; group*event interaction: F(11,6248) = 2.17, p>0.05; group*event*region interaction: F(11,6248) = 1.67, p>0.1).
source: When looking at the normalized activity in DMS and DLS in rats more or less sensitive to outcome devaluation during extended training, we found no significant differences (Figure 8B; main effect of group: F(1,568)=2.84, p>0.05; group*region interaction: F(1,568)=1.32, p>0.1; group*event interaction: F(11,6248) = 2.17, p>0.05; group*event*region interaction: F(11,6248) = 1.67, p>0.1).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Inactivation of DMS resulted in a subtle but significant decrease in the number of lever presses (F(1,7)=7.36, p<0.05).
source: Inactivation of DMS resulted in a subtle but significant decrease in the number of lever presses (Figure 9C; F(1,7)=7.36, p<0.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 9C.

claim: There was a trend toward an increase in latency to the first lever press following DMS inactivation (F(1,7)=5.16, p=0.057).
source: We also observed a trend toward an increase in latency to the first lever press following DMS inactivation (Figure 9D; F(1,7)=5.16, p=0.057), but no effect on response rate (Figure 9E; F(1,7)=1.43, p>0.1).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 9D.

claim: DMS inactivation had no effect on response rate (F(1,7)=1.43, p>0.1).
source: We also observed a trend toward an increase in latency to the first lever press following DMS inactivation (Figure 9D; F(1,7)=5.16, p=0.057), but no effect on response rate (Figure 9E; F(1,7)=1.43, p>0.1).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 9E.

claim: DLS inactivation slightly decreased the number of lever presses, although the effect was not significant (Sign test: Z11 = 1.8, p=0.07).
source: DLS inactivation slightly decreased the number of lever presses, although the effect was not significant (Figure 9F; Sign test: Z11 = 1.8, p=0.07).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 9F.

claim: A decrease in response rate was observed following DLS inactivation (F(1,10)=5.51, p<0.05).
source: We also observed a decrease in response rate following DLS inactivation (Figure 9H; F(1,10)=5.51, p<0.05), but no effect on the first lever press latency (Figure 9G; Sign test: Z11 = 0.6, p>0.5).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 9H.

claim: DLS inactivation had no effect on the first lever press latency (Sign test: Z11 = 0.6, p>0.5).
source: We also observed a decrease in response rate following DLS inactivation (Figure 9H; F(1,10)=5.51, p<0.05), but no effect on the first lever press latency (Figure 9G; Sign test: Z11 = 0.6, p>0.5).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 9G.

claim: The effect on response rate following DLS inactivation may result from a shift in the distribution of inter-press intervals to the right (K-S test: Dn = 0.17, p<0.0001).
source: The effect on response rate may result from a shift in the distribution of inter-press intervals to the right following DLS inactivation (Figure 9J; K-S test: Dn = 0.17, p<0.0001) but not DMS inactivation (Figure 9I; K-S test: Dn = 0.04, p>0.1).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 9J.

claim: DMS inactivation did not result in a shift in the distribution of inter-press intervals (K-S test: Dn = 0.04, p>0.1).
source: The effect on response rate may result from a shift in the distribution of inter-press intervals to the right following DLS inactivation (Figure 9J; K-S test: Dn = 0.17, p<0.0001) but not DMS inactivation (Figure 9I; K-S test: Dn = 0.04, p>0.1).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 9I.

claim: The inactivation results confirm the concurrent involvement of both DMS and DLS during sequence performance in the DT5-task.
source: These results confirm the concurrent involvement of both DMS and DLS during sequence performance in the DT5-task.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the inactivation experiment results.

claim: Spike activity of 42% of recorded MSNs in DLS and DMS was correlated with performance.
source: We found that spike activity of 42% of recorded MSNs in DLS and DMS was correlated with performance (Figure 10D), with significant regional differences (χ2=9.4, p<0.05; Figure 10E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 10D and 10E.

claim: There were significant regional differences in the proportion of neurons correlated with performance (χ2=9.4, p<0.05).
source: We found that spike activity of 42% of recorded MSNs in DLS and DMS was correlated with performance (Figure 10D), with significant regional differences (χ2=9.4, p<0.05; Figure 10E).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 10E.

claim: There was no significant difference between DMS and DLS in the proportion of neurons correlated with latency to 1st lever press (DLS: 16.6%, N = 56; DMS: 18.8%, N = 77) or response rate (DLS: 14.8%, N = 50; DMS: 13.7%, N = 56).
source: There was no significant difference between DMS and DLS in the proportion of neurons correlated with latency to 1st lever press (DLS: 16.6%, N = 56; DMS: 18.8%, N = 77) or response rate (DLS: 14.8%, N = 50; DMS: 13.7%, N = 56; Figure 10E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 10E.

claim: The proportion of neurons correlated with port entry latency was higher in DMS than DLS (DLS: 6.8%, N = 23; DMS: 11.9%, N = 49; χ2 = 5.6, p<0.05).
source: However, the proportion of neurons correlated with port entry latency was surprisingly higher in DMS than DLS (DLS: 6.8%, N = 23; DMS: 11.9%, N = 49; χ2 = 5.6, p<0.05; Figure 10E).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 10E.

claim: DMS activity remains correlated with optimized performance, and appears more involved at the termination of the behavioral sequence than DLS.
source: Thus, DMS activity remains correlated with optimized performance, and appears in fact more involved at the termination of the behavioral sequence than DLS.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the correlation analysis results.

claim: Correlated neurons were represented in every class of neuronal response, suggesting that each of the sequence-related activity patterns isolated in this study may contribute to ongoing performance in the DT5 task.
source: Correlated neurons were represented in every class of neuronal response determined above (Figure 10—figure supplement 1), suggesting that each of the sequence-related activity patterns isolated in this study may contribute to ongoing performance in the DT5 task.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 1.

claim: Rats trained in the DT5 procedure rapidly develop automated lever pressing behavior that is relatively insensitive to reward devaluation, a finding taken to indicate habitual control.
source: We have previously shown that rats trained in this procedure rapidly develop automated lever pressing behavior that is relatively insensitive to reward devaluation, a finding taken to indicate habitual control (Vandaele et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the authors' prior work.

claim: Both sustained excitation throughout sequentially-performed actions and excitation marking the beginning and termination of sequentially-performed actions have been proposed to represent the chunking of individual actions into a single unit.
source: Both sustained excitation throughout sequentially-performed actions and excitation marking the beginning and termination of sequentially-performed actions have been proposed to represent the chunking of individual actions into a single unit (Barnes et al., 2005; Graybiel and Grafton, 2015; Jin and Costa, 2015; Jin and Costa, 2010; Jin et al., 2014; Smith and Graybiel, 2016), while excitations at the boundaries of sequences have been hypothesized to signal the initiation and termination of the sequence (Jin et al., 2014; Jin and Costa, 2010; Jin and Costa, 2015; but see Sales-Carbonell et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Excitations at the boundaries of sequences have been hypothesized to signal the initiation and termination of the sequence.
source: Both sustained excitation throughout sequentially-performed actions and excitation marking the beginning and termination of sequentially-performed actions have been proposed to represent the chunking of individual actions into a single unit (Barnes et al., 2005; Graybiel and Grafton, 2015; Jin and Costa, 2015; Jin and Costa, 2010; Jin et al., 2014; Smith and Graybiel, 2016), while excitations at the boundaries of sequences have been hypothesized to signal the initiation and termination of the sequence (Jin et al., 2014; Jin and Costa, 2010; Jin and Costa, 2015; but see Sales-Carbonell et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Previous work has demonstrated the development of task-bracketing activity in DLS, but not in DMS, as rats learned to navigate in a T-maze.
source: Previous work has demonstrated the development of task-bracketing activity in DLS, but not in DMS, as rats learned to navigate in a T-maze (Barnes et al., 2005; Regier et al., 2015; Smith and Graybiel, 2013; Thorn et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In the study of Thorn and colleagues, DLS activity was characterized by excitation at the boundaries of the navigation sequence whereas DMS activity peaked in the middle, when animals chose between two directions based on instruction cues.
source: Indeed, in the study of Thorn and colleagues, DLS activity was characterized by excitation at the boundaries of the navigation sequence whereas DMS activity peaked in the middle, when animals chose between two directions based on instruction cues.
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to prior work by Thorn and colleagues.

claim: A study by Martiros et al. (2018) reported neuronal excitation at the beginning and end of a 3-response lever press sequence in the DLS, but not in the DMS.
source: A more recent study by Martiros et al. (2018) also reported neuronal excitation at the beginning and end of a 3-response lever press sequence in the DLS, but not in the DMS.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Both sustained excitation and inhibition were observed in the dorsal striatum of mice performing a series of lever presses.
source: In agreement with this notion, both sustained excitation and inhibition were observed in the dorsal striatum of mice similarly performing a series of lever presses (Jin and Costa, 2010; Jin et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Sustained excitation in DLS neurons is consistent with studies recording DLS activity in tasks involving locomotor sequences.
source: Sustained excitation in DLS neurons is also consistent with studies recording DLS activity in tasks involving locomotor sequences (Rueda-Orozco and Robbe, 2015; Sales-Carbonell et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: A prior study showed an absence of start signals at the initiation of a locomotor sequence.
source: This result is consistent with prior findings showing an absence of start signals at the initiation of a locomotor sequence (Sales-Carbonell et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Rats trained with both sucrose and pellets reliably show insensitivity to reward devalution by conditioned taste aversion.
source: We also note that rats trained with both sucrose and pellets reliably show insensitivity to reward devalution by conditioned taste aversion (Vandaele et al., 2017), supporting the notion that on average the DT5 procedure promotes habitual responding.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the authors' prior work.

claim: Skill learning is generally characterized by an initial phase of rapid performance improvement followed by an extended period of slow performance optimization (skill consolidation).
source: Skill learning is generally characterized by an initial phase of rapid performance improvement followed by an extended period of slow performance optimization (skill consolidation).
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge.

claim: The dorsal striatum plays a pivotal role in learning and performing actions, including sequential actions, made to obtain rewarding outcomes.
source: The dorsal striatum plays a pivotal role in learning and performing actions, including sequential actions, made to obtain rewarding outcomes, with distinct functions proposed for different striatal subregions (Balleine et al., 2009; Graybiel and Grafton, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Distinct functions are proposed for different striatal subregions.
source: The dorsal striatum plays a pivotal role in learning and performing actions, including sequential actions, made to obtain rewarding outcomes, with distinct functions proposed for different striatal subregions (Balleine et al., 2009; Graybiel and Grafton, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: It is not clear how behavior-related neural activity in DMS and DLS relates to behavioral improvement over time.
source: More broadly, it is not clear how behavior-related neural activity in DMS and DLS relates to behavioral improvement over time.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The DLS task-bracketing activity during navigational sequences is similar to that observed during acquisition of lever-pressing sequences and likewise may reflect chunking.
source: The DLS task-bracketing activity during navigational sequences is similar to that observed during acquisition of lever-pressing sequences and likewise may reflect chunking (Redish, 2016; Smith and Graybiel, 2014; Smith and Graybiel, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Rats were given the opportunity to respond on 30 trials separated by 1 min intertrial intervals in the DT5 task.
source: Rats were given the opportunity to respond on 30 trials separated by 1 min intertrial intervals.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure.

claim: In the DT5 task, each trial began with lever insertion after which rats were required to complete a sequence of 5 lever presses to obtain access to reward, signaled by lever retraction after the fifth lever press.
source: In this task, each trial began with lever insertion after which rats were required to complete a sequence of 5 lever presses to obtain access to reward, signaled by lever retraction after the fifth lever press (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure shown in Figure 1A.

claim: One group of rats was implanted with fixed recording electrodes in the DMS and DLS before training in the DT5 task (early training group, N = 9).
source: To measure neural activity during learning, one group of rats was implanted with fixed recording electrodes in the DMS and DLS before training in the DT5 task, and neural activity in these regions was recorded during acquisition (early training group, N = 9).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure.

claim: Rats in the second group were implanted in the DMS and DLS with drivable recording electrodes after more than 8 weeks of training in the DT5 procedure (extended training group, N = 8).
source: To measure neural activity in well-trained subjects, rats in the second group were implanted in the DMS and DLS with drivable recording electrodes after more than 8 weeks of training in the DT5 procedure (extended training group, N = 8; Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure.

claim: Electrode placements were similar in the early and extended training groups.
source: Electrode placements were similar in the early and extended training groups (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Putative medium spiny neuron (MSN) and interneuron populations were distinguished using firing rates and waveform properties.
source: To focus on the primary population of striatal neurons, putative medium spiny neuron (MSN) and interneuron populations were distinguished using firing rates and waveform properties (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D–F; Martiros et al., 2018; Schmitzer-Torbert and Redish, 2008; Stalnaker et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a description of the analytical method used, supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Neurons not classified as putative-FSI but showing features intermediate to MSN and FSI were unclassified (early training, N = 1–9 per session; extended training, N = 74).
source: Neurons not classified as putative-FSI but showing features intermediate to MSN and FSI were unclassified (early training, N = 1–9 per session; extended training, N = 74).
evidence: This is a description of the analytical method used.

claim: Putative tonically active neurons (TANs) could not be reliably isolated based on waveform.
source: As reported previously, we could not reliably isolate putative tonically active neurons (TANs) based on waveform (Sales-Carbonell et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: TANs represent about 1% of neurons in dorsal striatum.
source: Given the low number of TANs in dorsal striatum (about 1%; Oorschot, 2013; Schmitzer-Torbert and Redish, 2008), we assumed any possible misclassification of TANs as MSNs, though unlikely, would have minimal impact on the population characteristics presented in this study.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The study focused only on the putative MSN population.
source: In this paper we focus only on the putative MSN population.
evidence: This is a statement about the scope of the study.

claim: The over-representation of sustained excitation in the DLS, and of sustained inhibition in the DMS likely explains the regional differences observed in the analysis of the average activity during the first and last early training sessions.
source: Overall, these results show that DMS and DLS neurons express similar types of behavioral correlates during early training, but with large differences in their relative proportions. This over-representation of sustained excitation in the DLS, and of sustained inhibition in the DMS likely explains the regional differences observed in the analysis of the average activity during the first and last early training sessions (Figure 2).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The increase in similarity between DMS and DLS after extended training appears to mainly result from differences in sustained activity responses.
source: This classification analysis looking at individual neuronal responses confirms the findings based on average ensemble activity in showing that DMS and DLS activity differs during early training and is much more similar after extended training. This increase in similarity appears to mainly result from differences in sustained activity responses.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the classification analysis results.

claim: After extended training, there is a higher proportion of INH response patterns in DLS and a higher proportion of EXC response patterns in DMS relative to early training leading to similar average responding.
source: After extended training, there is a higher proportion of INH response patterns in DLS and a higher proportion of EXC response patterns in DMS relative to early training leading to similar average responding.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data from the study.

claim: The difference in proportions of neuron subtypes across DLS and DMS in early training permits a reliable inference of which region a neuron comes from when using an unbiased decoding strategy.
source: These findings are consistent with the differences in proportions of neuron subtypes across the two regions in early training; this difference in proportions permits a reliable inference of which region a neuron comes from when using an unbiased decoding strategy.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the decoding analysis results.

claim: DMS and DLS activity was relatively dissimilar during early training but similar after extended training, as demonstrated through three approaches.
source: Altogether, these findings demonstrate through three approaches that DMS and DLS activity was relatively dissimilar during early training but similar after extended training.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings.

claim: The specific DMS and DLS neural patterns observed during the first 10 DT5 sessions do not substantially correlate with the presence or absence of habitual control.
source: However, our analysis suggests that the specific DMS and DLS neural patterns observed during those 10 sessions do not substantially correlate with the presence or absence of habitual control, because when we separated subjects based on habitual or goal-directed control for early (or extended) training, the neural patterns were largely similar.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data analysis.

claim: It is not clear whether or how sequence-related activity relates to either skill learning/performance or habit learning/performance.
source: Overall, it is not clear whether or how sequence-related activity relates to either skill learning/performance or habit learning/performance.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the study's findings.

claim: Future studies could address the question of how sequence-related activity relates to skill or habit learning by comparing dorsostriatal activity in the DT5 task with free-running instrumental behavior that remains goal directed after extended training.
source: Future studies could address this question by comparing dorsostriatal activity in the DT5 task with free-running instrumental behavior that remains goal directed after extended training (Vandaele et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a suggestion for future research.

claim: All subjects experienced prior instrumental training under CRF and DT1 during which relevant aspects of the behavior and neural activity may have become organized.
source: We focused on neural activity at the beginning of DT5 training, but all subjects experienced prior instrumental training under CRF and DT1 during which relevant aspects of the behavior and neural activity may have become organized.
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental procedure and a speculation about its effects.

claim: In the DT5 task, rats do not have to track the number of presses emitted to obtain the reward and may just continue pressing on the lever until its retraction, which may favor behavioral chunking and the specific activity patterns reported in this study.
source: In fact, in the DT5 task, rats do not have to track the number of presses emitted to obtain the reward and may just continue pressing on the lever until its retraction, which may favor behavioral chunking and the specific activity patterns reported in this study.
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanisms underlying the observed behavior and neural activity.

claim: Rapid acquisition of the new response requirement, facilitated by the presence of cues predicting reward availability and delivery, could explain why sequence-related activity is observed in both regions very rapidly, compared to previous studies using uncued, self-paced procedures or requiring discriminatory learning.
source: Thus, rapid acquisition of the new response requirement, facilitated by the presence of cues predicting reward availability and delivery, could explain why sequence-related activity is observed in both regions very rapidly, compared to previous studies using uncued, self-paced procedures or requiring discriminatory learning (Barnes et al., 2005; Jin and Costa, 2010; Jin et al., 2014; Smith and Graybiel, 2013; Thorn et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanisms underlying the observed neural activity, with reference to prior work.

claim: Including probe trials in which lever retraction is delayed would be helpful for determining to what extent behavior and neural activity depend on the lever retraction cue.
source: Including probe trials in which lever retraction is delayed would be helpful for to determining to what extent behavior and neural activity depend on the lever retraction cue.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future research.

claim: During extended training, execution of lever press sequences was optimized and stereotyped, with within-sequence response rate, trial-by-trial variability in response rate, and 1st lever press latency reaching asymptotic levels.
source: We observed that during extended training, execution of lever press sequences was optimized and stereotyped, with within-sequence response rate, trial-by-trial variability in response rate, and 1st lever press latency reaching asymptotic levels.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the study.

claim: Ensemble activity analysis revealed that, on average, both DMS and DLS expressed sustained excitation throughout the lever press sequence with peaks following lever insertion and retraction after extended training.
source: Ensemble activity analysis revealed that, on average, both DMS and DLS expressed sustained excitation throughout the lever press sequence with peaks following lever insertion and retraction.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the study.

claim: Less activity during lever presses and stronger activity in response to lever insertion and retraction was observed in Phasic DLS neurons after extended training compared to early training.
source: Furthermore, we observed less activity during lever presses and stronger activity in response to lever insertion and retraction in Phasic DLS neurons after extended training compared to early training (compare Figure 3C–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 3C-D.

claim: One interpretation is that changes in neural activity after extended training reflect greater cue encoding in DLS and greater action encoding in DMS.
source: One interpretation is that these changes reflect greater cue encoding in DLS and greater action encoding in DMS.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data.

claim: Skill consolidation following many weeks of training in this task leads to improved integration of both cues and actions across regions within the dorsal striatum.
source: This suggests that skill consolidation following many weeks of training in this task leads to improved integration of both cues and actions across regions within the dorsal striatum.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data.

claim: Few studies have examined neuronal activity in dorsal striatum across two training stages so separated in time.
source: Few studies have examined neuronal activity in dorsal striatum across two training stages so separated in time, so it is not yet clear whether findings will be similar after extended training (months) in other tasks.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The relative absence of change across early training may reflect rapid behavioral chunking promoted by the lever insertion and retraction cues.
source: One interpretation is that the absence of change across early training reflects rapid behavioral chunking promoted by the lever insertion and retraction cues.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: The alterations in sequence-related activity over extended training may reflect a refinement of the temporal properties of striatal circuit engagement that may not map one-to-one with the behavioral variables typically measured.
source: Furthermore, the alterations in sequence-related activity over extended training may reflect a refinement of the temporal properties of striatal circuit engagement that may not map one-to-one with the behavioral variables we and others typically measure.
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanisms underlying the observed neural activity changes.

claim: It is possible that temporally-correlated circuit engagement across parallel corticostriatal loops is associated with better performance and/or skill consolidation, but this remains to be tested.
source: It is possible that temporally-correlated circuit engagement across parallel corticostriatal loops is associated with better performance and/or skill consolidation, but this remains to be tested.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential mechanisms.

claim: Sequence-related activity in the dorsal striatum during early and extended training may reflect additional processes not captured by behavioral indicators of sequence learning, optimization of performance, or habits.
source: Together, these findings suggest that sequence-related activity in the dorsal striatum during early and extended training may reflect additional processes not captured by our behavioral indicators of sequence learning, optimization of performance, or habits.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: The functional contribution of DMS and DLS signals to behavior is expected to be distinct based on the specific connectivity of these regions as nodes within parallel corticostriatal loops.
source: While the proportions of distinct classes of neuronal activity patterns that might represent chunking were different in DLS and DMS, both regions do show these types of patterns, and these patterns were similar after extended training. Yet, the functional contribution of these DMS and DLS signals to behavior is expected to be distinct based on the specific connectivity of these regions as nodes within parallel corticostriatal loops.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge about striatal connectivity.

claim: DMS neural activity may mediate the impact of associations between the lever retraction stimulus or the port entry action with the rewarding outcome even after substantial training.
source: After extended training, a greater proportion of DMS than DLS neurons showed significant trial-by-trial correlations between neuronal activity after the final lever press and latency to enter the reward port. This suggests that DMS neural activity may mediate the impact of associations between the lever retraction stimulus or the port entry action with the rewarding outcome (Burton et al., 2015; Ito and Doya, 2015; Kimchi and Laubach, 2009b; Kimchi and Laubach, 2009a) even after substantial training.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the correlation analysis results, supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Both DLS and DMS are involved at the initiation and execution of the sequence.
source: Interestingly, similar proportions of neurons in DMS and DLS expressed correlations with the 1st lever press latency and the response rate, suggesting that both regions are involved at the initiation and execution of the sequence.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the correlation analysis results.

claim: The correlation analyses and the inactivations support a role for sensorimotor striatal activity in moment-by-moment expression of behavior.
source: Taken together, the correlation analyses and the inactivations support a role for sensorimotor striatal activity in moment-by-moment expression of behavior (Robbe, 2018; Rueda-Orozco and Robbe, 2015; Sales-Carbonell et al., 2018), suggesting that the neural representation of higher-order functions, including transitions in cognitive control, may be more clearly reflected in activity in other regions, or in broader neuronal loops that include the striatum.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings, supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The neural representation of higher-order functions, including transitions in cognitive control, may be more clearly reflected in activity in other regions, or in broader neuronal loops that include the striatum.
source: Taken together, the correlation analyses and the inactivations support a role for sensorimotor striatal activity in moment-by-moment expression of behavior (Robbe, 2018; Rueda-Orozco and Robbe, 2015; Sales-Carbonell et al., 2018), suggesting that the neural representation of higher-order functions, including transitions in cognitive control, may be more clearly reflected in activity in other regions, or in broader neuronal loops that include the striatum.
